newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees progress in crucial Korea meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees progress in crucial Korea meeting.

text.p: A crucial meeting on Korean peninsula peace efforts opened on Wednesday with the United States reporting early progress and predicting a conclusion by day's end.

"We're encouraged by the early progress that has been made," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said after two hours of talks at a swanky Manhattan hotel between delegations from the two Koreas and the United States.

He said he expected statements from all three participants when the talks end during the afternoon. The meeting was called to answer the question of whether famine-threatened Stalinist North Korea was prepared to make a serious bid for peace with its prosperous democratic arch-rival in the south.

U.S. officials have been optimistic Pyongyang would respond positively to Washington's year-old joint proposal with South Korea for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War, replacing a fraying armistice with a peace treaty. China would also participate.

"We hope very much that as a result of these talks North Korea will decide to agree with the four-party proposal," Burns told reporters in Washington. He based his upbeat assessment on a telephone conversation with the chief U.S. negotiator, Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Charles Kartman, during a lunch break in the talks.

"The talks are under way on a trilateral basis. They're going well. We're certainly encouraged by the first few hours of the talks and we hope very much for a positive result from these discussions," Burns said.

North Korea publicly was upbeat as the meeting began. "I think we will come out with good results," Kim Gye Gwan, Pyongyang's delegation chief, told his South Korean counterpart during a picture-taking session with journalists.

Seoul's chief negotiator Song Young Shik was also in an jovial mood, laughing, engaging in chit-chat with Kim and saying he hoped the meeting would reflect the warm spring day that had enveloped New York.
North and South Korean delegation leaders, smiling broadly, joined in a three-way handshake with Kartman.
Asked by reporters how he thought the meeting would go, Song held up his crossed fingers, a sign that he hoped the results would be positive.

During the lunchtime break, another South Korean official, Ji Won Suk, told reporters he was encouraged but the North Koreans had not given their formal response to the four-party peace talks proposal. The morning session involved Pyongyang making a "presentation," he said.
As the meeting began, Song told Kim: "So we are at the middle of a warm spring and I hope that this meeting will also be very cosy and a very ... productive spring."
Kim replied: "There is a saying that beginnings are half done so we have right now started our meeting and so I think we will come out with good results."
U.S. and South Korean negotiators were ready for marathon talks that would not produce a conclusive reply until Friday. But Burns indicated the extra session would not be needed.

It was thought North Korea might make a final pitch for more food aid after two years of shortages due to flooding that the United States, as well as humanitarian groups, agreed are devastating and worsening.
If Pyongyang agreed, the landmark peace talks would not begin until June or July. The goal was to defuse tensions on the heavily armed and volatile divided Korean peninsula.

On the eve of the crucial meeting, the United States announced $15 million in additional food aid to feed children in North Korea. It said the donation, which brings total U.S. food aid to Pyongyang to $33.4 million since late 1995, was made because food shortages would be critical this spring.
